You see, I'd stored my handkerchief inside my helmet, along with a few other things. But this was the kind of helmet you couldn't remove without help. That hadn't crossed my mind when I put it there; in fact, I hadn't known. I'd thought it would be a wonderfully convenient place. So knowing it was right there, so close and handy but impossible to reach, only made the misery worse. The thing you can't have is generally the thing you want most; everyone has noticed that. It drove every other thought from my head and fixed my attention entirely on the helmet. Mile after mile, my mind stayed there, imagining that handkerchief, seeing it before me. Meanwhile salty sweat kept running into my eyes, and I couldn't get at the thing. It was maddening. Written down, it sounds like a small problem, but it wasn't small at all. It was real, thorough misery, and I wouldn't say so if it weren't true. I decided that next time I'd bring a little handbag, however it looked and whatever anybody said. Of course those iron-clad fashion plates of the Round Table would consider it disgraceful and perhaps raise hell about it. But I wanted comfort first and style afterward. We kept jogging along, sometimes crossing dusty stretches where clouds rose around us. The dust filled my nose and made me sneeze and weep, and naturally I said things I shouldn't have. I don't deny it. I'm no better than anyone else.

We couldn't seem to find a soul in this deserted Britain, not even an ogre. Given my mood, that was lucky for the ogre—especially if he carried a handkerchief. Most knights would have cared only about taking his armour. I'd have let him keep all his metalwork if I could just have his bandanna.

Meanwhile, it grew hotter and hotter inside my suit. The sun kept beating down, heating the iron more with every minute. When you're that hot, every little thing gets on your nerves. At a trot I rattled like a box of crockery, which annoyed me. And I could hardly bear the shield flapping and banging, first against my chest and then around my back. If I slowed to a walk, the joints of the armour squeaked and screeched like an irritating wheelbarrow. At that speed we stirred no breeze, so I felt about to fry inside my stove. Besides, the more slowly we moved, the heavier the iron settled upon me, until every minute I seemed to weigh several more tons.

Raymond paced angrily across the room. I stood waiting, ready to hear his accusations and answer them. Adrian leaned against the wall. 'This is completely ridiculous,' he exclaimed. 'Even schoolboys couldn't behave more unreasonably.'

'You don't understand,' Raymond said. 'This is part of a whole system—a plan to control me that I will never accept. Because I am Protector of England, must I be the only slave in its empire? Must people invade my privacy, criticize my actions, and insult my friends? I'll free myself from all of it. Bear witness!' He pulled the star that marked his office from his chest and threw it onto the table. 'I give up my office. I surrender my power. Let anyone who wants it take it!'

'Let someone take it,' Adrian exclaimed, 'who can claim to be better than you, or whom the world considers better. No man in England is arrogant enough to make that claim. Recognize your own worth, Raymond, and your anger will pass; your confidence will return. A few months ago, whenever we prayed for our country's prosperity or our own, we also prayed for the Protector's life and happiness, because they seemed inseparable. You spent your days working for our benefit; your ambition was to earn our praise. You gave our towns beautiful buildings and useful institutions. You made our land richly productive. The powerful and unjust trembled before your judgment, while the poor and oppressed flourished under your protection like flowers opening in the morning sun.

'Can you wonder that we feel shocked and grieve when all that seems changed? Come, this burst of anger has already passed. Return to your duties. Your supporters will welcome you, your enemies will fall silent, and we will show you our love, respect, and loyalty again. Control yourself, Raymond, and you can command the world.'

'That would be sensible advice for someone else,' Raymond answered gloomily. 'Learn the lesson yourself, and you, the country's highest nobleman, may become its ruler. You are good, wise, and just; you could rule every heart. But I now see, too soon for my own happiness and too late for England's benefit, that I accepted a task beyond my abilities. I cannot control myself. My passions rule me; my slightest impulse is a tyrant. Do you think I gave up the Protectorate—and I have given it up—in a moment of temper? By the living God, I swear never to pick up that trinket again. Never again will I carry the burden of worry and misery it represents.'

Recent reports from Rotterdam suggest that the city is in a state of great scientific excitement. Things have happened there that were so unexpected, so entirely new, and so opposed to established ideas that I feel sure all Europe must already be in an uproar. Physics must be in turmoil, with reason and astronomy at each other's throats.

It seems that on the —— day of ——, though I cannot be certain of the date, a vast crowd gathered in the great Exchange square of that well-ordered city. Their purpose was not clearly stated. The weather was warm, unusually warm for the season, and scarcely a breath of wind stirred. The crowd did not mind the occasional brief, refreshing showers falling from great white clouds scattered across the blue sky. Around noon, however, a small but noticeable stir passed through the gathering. Ten thousand voices began chattering. A moment later, ten thousand faces looked skyward, ten thousand pipes dropped at once from the corners of ten thousand mouths, and a shout like the roar of Niagara rang loudly, fiercely, and for a long time through Rotterdam and its surroundings.

The cause of the commotion soon became clear. From behind one of those enormous, sharply outlined clouds, a strange collection of apparently solid materials slowly emerged into a patch of open blue. Its shape was so peculiar, and its parts fitted together so fancifully, that the sturdy townspeople staring open-mouthed below could neither understand it nor finish marvelling at it. What could it be? In the name of every woman and devil in Rotterdam, what could it possibly mean? Nobody knew. Nobody could even guess. Not a soul—not even the mayor, Mynheer Superbus Von Underduk—had the slightest clue to solve the mystery. Since there was nothing more sensible to do, every man carefully returned his pipe to the corner of his mouth. Each turned his right eye up toward the strange sight, puffed, paused, waddled about, and gave a meaningful grunt. Then he waddled back, grunted, paused, and finally puffed again.

Meanwhile the object that had caused so much curiosity, and so much smoke, continued descending toward the fine city. In just a few minutes it came close enough for everyone to make it out clearly. It looked like—yes, it certainly was—a kind of balloon. But surely nobody in Rotterdam had ever seen a balloon like this before.
